conversation_lines.speaker: Doctor
conversation_lines.text: Hello, I’m Dr. Lee, one of your nephrology team members. I understand you came in today because your kidney function was off during your clinic visit?

conversation_lines.speaker: Patient
conversation_lines.text: Yes, that’s right. My creatinine was higher than usual—2.9 instead of my normal 1.7. But I feel fine, no symptoms at all.

conversation_lines.speaker: Doctor
conversation_lines.text: That’s good you’re feeling well. But a jump like that does raise concern, especially with your history. We’re admitting you to check for possible rejection of your transplant.

conversation_lines.speaker: Patient
conversation_lines.text: Rejection? I thought I was stable. I’ve been careful with my meds.

conversation_lines.speaker: Doctor
conversation_lines.text: You have been, and that helps a lot. But sometimes rejection can happen even when we’re doing everything right. We’ll do an ultrasound first to look at the kidney.

conversation_lines.speaker: Doctor
conversation_lines.text: The ultrasound is back. There’s mild hydronephrosis—some swelling in the kidney—and the blood flow looks a bit stiff. That supports the need to look closer.

conversation_lines.speaker: Patient
conversation_lines.text: Swelling? Is that serious?

conversation_lines.speaker: Doctor
conversation_lines.text: It’s mild, so not an emergency, but it’s a clue. We still need a biopsy to know for sure what’s going on. We’ll do that tomorrow morning.

conversation_lines.speaker: Patient
conversation_lines.text: A biopsy? Is that risky?

conversation_lines.speaker: Doctor
conversation_lines.text: It’s a small needle biopsy, guided by ultrasound. Very safe. We’ll take a tiny piece of the kidney to examine under the microscope.

conversation_lines.speaker: Doctor
conversation_lines.text: Good morning. We’re all set for the biopsy. You’ll lie on your stomach, and we’ll use the ultrasound to guide the needle.

conversation_lines.speaker: Patient
conversation_lines.text: Okay, I’m ready. Just tell me what to do.

conversation_lines.speaker: Doctor
conversation_lines.text: All done. Two samples were taken, sent to pathology. You’ll need to lie flat for a few hours to prevent bleeding.

conversation_lines.speaker: Patient
conversation_lines.text: That wasn’t so bad. How long until we know the results?

conversation_lines.speaker: Doctor
conversation_lines.text: We should have preliminary findings by tomorrow, full report in a few days. We’ll start watching your labs closely.

conversation_lines.speaker: Doctor
conversation_lines.text: The biopsy shows acute humoral rejection. That means your immune system is attacking the kidney, even though you’re on anti-rejection meds.

conversation_lines.speaker: Patient
conversation_lines.text: Oh no. I lost my first kidney to rejection. I don’t want to lose this one.

conversation_lines.speaker: Doctor
conversation_lines.text: We’re going to treat this aggressively to protect it. We’ll start plasmapheresis—cleaning antibodies out of your blood—and high-dose steroids.

conversation_lines.speaker: Patient
conversation_lines.text: Plasma-what? That sounds intense.

conversation_lines.speaker: Doctor
conversation_lines.text: It is, but it’s standard for this type of rejection. We’ll place a temporary catheter in your neck to run the treatment.

conversation_lines.speaker: Doctor
conversation_lines.text: The catheter is in—right internal jugular. You’ll start plasmapheresis this afternoon.

conversation_lines.speaker: Patient
conversation_lines.text: It’s in already? I didn’t feel much.

conversation_lines.speaker: Doctor
conversation_lines.text: You were given some sedation. You’ll have sessions every other day. We’re also starting IV steroids—500 mg daily for three days.

conversation_lines.speaker: Doctor
conversation_lines.text: How are you feeling this morning?

conversation_lines.speaker: Patient
conversation_lines.text: A bit jittery. And I’m hungry, but my blood sugar was high this morning.

conversation_lines.speaker: Doctor
conversation_lines.text: The steroids can raise blood sugar. We’re starting glipizide twice a day and will check your sugars four times daily.

conversation_lines.speaker: Patient
conversation_lines.text: I’ve never had diabetes. Is this permanent?

conversation_lines.speaker: Doctor
conversation_lines.text: Not necessarily. It might improve as we lower the steroid dose. We’ll monitor closely.

conversation_lines.speaker: Doctor
conversation_lines.text: Your blood pressure has been running high—around 165/90. We think it’s from the steroids and fluid from plasmapheresis.

conversation_lines.speaker: Patient
conversation_lines.text: I’ve always had high BP, but it’s usually controlled.

conversation_lines.speaker: Doctor
conversation_lines.text: We’re increasing your labetalol to 600 mg three times a day and adding furosemide 20 mg twice daily to help with fluid.

conversation_lines.speaker: Patient
conversation_lines.text: Okay. I have noticed my ankles are a little puffy.

conversation_lines.speaker: Doctor
conversation_lines.text: You’ve had your second plasmapheresis. How are you feeling?

conversation_lines.speaker: Patient
conversation_lines.text: Tired, but my breathing feels better. Less tight.

conversation_lines.speaker: Doctor
conversation_lines.text: Good—that’s probably the fluid coming down. Your BP is improving too, now around 140s/80s.

conversation_lines.speaker: Doctor
conversation_lines.text: Your creatinine is still high—2.7—and not coming down as fast as we’d like.

conversation_lines.speaker: Patient
conversation_lines.text: Does that mean the treatment isn’t working?

conversation_lines.speaker: Doctor
conversation_lines.text: Not necessarily. We’re adding a medication called ATG—anti-thymocyte globulin—to further calm your immune system.

conversation_lines.speaker: Patient
conversation_lines.text: More treatment? How many more things will I need?

conversation_lines.speaker: Doctor
conversation_lines.text: Just four doses, given over the next few days. It’s strong, so we’ll watch for side effects like fever or low blood counts.

conversation_lines.speaker: Doctor
conversation_lines.text: Starting your first ATG infusion today. We’ll go slowly and monitor you closely.

conversation_lines.speaker: Patient
conversation_lines.text: I’m a little nervous. Any chance of fever?

conversation_lines.speaker: Doctor
conversation_lines.text: Possible, but we’ll give pre-medications to reduce that risk. Let us know right away if you feel chills or warmth.

conversation_lines.speaker: Doctor
conversation_lines.text: You’re halfway through ATG. No fevers, which is great. But your white count is dropping—down to 2.8.

conversation_lines.speaker: Patient
conversation_lines.text: Is that dangerous?

conversation_lines.speaker: Doctor
conversation_lines.text: It means you’re more prone to infection. We’ll keep an eye on it, but it’s expected with this treatment.

conversation_lines.speaker: Doctor
conversation_lines.text: Your third plasmapheresis is scheduled for today. Creatinine is still 2.6—stable but not improving yet.

conversation_lines.speaker: Patient
conversation_lines.text: I’m hoping it starts to come down soon.

conversation_lines.speaker: Doctor
conversation_lines.text: We are too. The treatment takes time. The fact that you’re feeling well is a good sign.

conversation_lines.speaker: Doctor
conversation_lines.text: Final ATG dose given yesterday. You’ve tolerated it well. We’re switching to oral prednisone—20 mg daily—and tapering down.

conversation_lines.speaker: Patient
conversation_lines.text: So I’ll be on steroids longer?

conversation_lines.speaker: Doctor
conversation_lines.text: Yes, but at a much lower dose than the IV. We’ll keep the glipizide and add Humalog insulin with meals to manage sugars.

conversation_lines.speaker: Patient
conversation_lines.text: Insulin? I really hope I don’t need that long-term.

conversation_lines.speaker: Doctor
conversation_lines.text: We’ll reassess when steroids are lower. For now, it’s to keep your sugars safe.

conversation_lines.speaker: Doctor
conversation_lines.text: We’re planning discharge tomorrow. You’ll go home with adjusted meds and close follow-up.

conversation_lines.speaker: Patient
conversation_lines.text: That’s a relief. What changes should I expect?

conversation_lines.speaker: Doctor
conversation_lines.text: We’re increasing tacrolimus to 6.5 mg twice daily, stopping lisinopril, and continuing the new BP and diabetes meds.

conversation_lines.speaker: Patient
conversation_lines.text: And the catheter?

conversation_lines.speaker: Doctor
conversation_lines.text: It will be removed just before you leave. You won’t need it anymore.

conversation_lines.speaker: Doctor
conversation_lines.text: Good morning. Final check before discharge. Your labs are stable, you’re feeling well, and the catheter is out.

conversation_lines.speaker: Patient
conversation_lines.text: I’m ready to go home. Thank you for everything.

conversation_lines.speaker: Doctor
conversation_lines.text: You did great. Keep taking all meds as prescribed, log your blood sugars, and see your transplant team in one week.

conversation_lines.speaker: Patient
conversation_lines.text: I will. I just hope this kidney holds on.

conversation_lines.speaker: Doctor
conversation_lines.text: We’re giving it the best chance. You’ve been through a lot, but you’re on the right path.

conversation_lines.speaker: Patient
conversation_lines.text: Thank you, Doctor. I really appreciate it.

conversation_lines.speaker: Doctor
conversation_lines.text: Take care. Call if you have fever, swelling, or blood sugar issues. We’re here for you.
